topics.name: regex
topics.description: Regex is a pattern language, not a shell command. Tools such as grep, sed, and awk use related but sometimes different regex dialects.

sections.title: In grep
sections.body: grep uses Basic Regex (BRE) by default. Use grep -E for Extended Regex (ERE), which supports familiar +, ?, |, and grouping (...) without extra backslashes. Use grep -o to print only matched substrings. Prefer single quotes around the pattern so Bash does not expand it.

sections.title: Core regex symbols
sections.body: In regex, punctuation can have special meanings:

items.definition: Matches one character (except a newline in common implementations).
Matches a literal dot; important for website domains.
Matches one ASCII letter or digit.
Repeats the preceding element one or more times with grep -E.
Repeats the preceding element zero or more times.
Makes the preceding element optional with grep -E.
Groups alternatives: either a or b with grep -E.
Match the start / end of a line.
POSIX character class for a digit (portable to POSIX regex).

sections.title: Literal dots in URLs
sections.body: A plain dot in regex matches any single character, so ynetnews.com would also match ynetnewsXcom. Write ynetnews\.com when you need an actual dot. A URL is just text being matched; grep does not open the URL.

sections.title: Which regex tester?
sections.body: The MDN cheat sheet documents JavaScript regex, not precisely grep's POSIX dialect. For grep -E, choose POSIX ERE in regex101 if available. Some JavaScript and PCRE-only features do not work in standard grep -E.

examples.description: Print lines containing cat or cot.
Print only the matching substring instead of entire lines.
Extract matching article URLs from HTML stored in page_data (if those URLs exist).

practice: Quote regex patterns with single quotes whenever you do not need shell expansion.
Use -E for extended regex, and -o when you only want the matching text.
Test patterns against real samples; regex flavors differ.

links.title: MDN: JavaScript regex cheat sheet
links.note: Syntax reference for JavaScript regex; not identical to grep.

links.title: regex101
links.note: Interactive tester; select the appropriate regex flavor.

topics.description: The equals sign is used for variable assignments, but its meaning depends on context. Assignment is shell syntax, not a standalone command.

sections.title: Variable assignment
sections.body: For a simple assignment, write name=value with NO spaces on either side of =. Spaces split words into separate shell arguments. Do not place $ before the variable name when assigning it.

sections.title: Reading a value
sections.body: Use $name or, more safely inside other text, ${name} to expand an existing variable. Use quotes around expansions to prevent unwanted word splitting and globbing.

sections.title: Not every equals sign is an assignment
sections.body: Inside [[ ... ]], = or == compares strings; inside (( ... )), = can assign arithmetic values. The spaces allowed in these constructs are different from ordinary variable assignments.

sections.title: Keep in mind
sections.body: Variables can store text, including the stdout of a command through $(...). Bash variables cannot hold NUL bytes; command substitution also removes trailing newline characters.

examples.description: Assign text, including a space, to name.
Print the value stored in name.
Store the response body sent to stdout in page_data.
Compare strings using a Bash conditional expression.

practice: No spaces around = for a plain assignment.
Write variable names without $ on the left side, and quote variable expansions when appropriate.

topics.name: quoting
topics.description: Quoting protects text from shell interpretation. Single and double quotes are useful for different reasons.

sections.title: Single quotes
sections.body: 'text' treats nearly everything inside literally. Even $HOME remains the characters $HOME. A single quote cannot be placed directly inside a single-quoted string.

sections.title: Double quotes
sections.body: "text" protects spaces and most shell metacharacters but still permits variable and command substitution, such as "$HOME" and "$(date)".

sections.title: Why quote URLs?
sections.body: An unquoted URL containing &, ?, * or spaces can be split or interpreted by Bash. Quoting URLs prevents these surprises. A simple URL may happen to work unquoted, but quoting is a reliable habit.

sections.title: Regex patterns
sections.body: Use single quotes for static regex patterns such as 'https://example\.com/[0-9]+'. The quotes are for Bash, not for enabling regex in grep.

examples.description: Keep the complete URL as one argument.
Safely print a variable that may contain spaces.
Pass the regex pattern to grep without shell expansion.

practice: Quote URLs and variable expansions by default.
Prefer single quotes for static regex; use double quotes when shell variables should expand.

topics.name: stdin / stdout / stderr
topics.summary: Understand where program input and output go
topics.description: Unix programs commonly use three standard streams: input (stdin), normal output (stdout), and error output (stderr).

sections.title: The three streams
sections.body: They are connections, not Bash variables. By default stdin reads from the terminal, while stdout and stderr are displayed in the terminal. A command may instead read from a file or another process.

items.definition: Normal program input; often supplied by typing or a pipe.
Normal output intended for data or results.
Diagnostics, warnings, and error messages.

sections.title: Redirection
sections.body: Use > for stdout to a file, 2> for stderr to a file, and < to read stdin from a file. A pipe connects one process's stdout to another process's stdin.

sections.title: Exit status is separate
sections.body: After a command finishes, Bash receives an exit status. Status 0 typically means success; a nonzero status signals a condition such as an error or no match. Exit status is not the text on stdout.

examples.description: Send grep error messages to a file while keeping normal output separate.
Pass stdout to wc as stdin.

practice: Do not assume everything displayed on screen is stdout.
Use 2> separately when you need error messages.

topics.name: pipes & redirection
topics.description: Bash operators route data between files, variables, and commands. They are shell syntax, not separate executables.

sections.title: Common operators
sections.body: Each operator has a different role:

items.definition: Connect the stdout of the command on the left to the stdin of the command on the right.
Write stdout to a file, overwriting it.
Append stdout to a file.
Write stderr to a file.
Read stdin from a file.
Bash here-string: send a string plus a newline to stdin.
Make stderr go to the same destination as stdout at that point in the command.

sections.title: Passing a variable to grep
sections.body: Writing grep PATTERN page_data means open a FILE named page_data. To search the CONTENTS of the variable, use grep PATTERN <<< "$page_data" instead.

sections.title: Order matters
sections.body: For example, command >out 2>&1 routes both streams to out. Reversing redirections can change their destinations.

examples.description: Search for digits in the text stored in a Bash variable.

practice: Use > carefully because it overwrites existing files.
Quote variables passed through here-strings.

topics.summary: Capture command output in a variable
topics.description: Command substitution runs a command and replaces $(...) with its stdout. This differs from simply expanding $variable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The shell executes the command inside $(...), captures stdout as text, removes trailing newlines, and substitutes the result into the surrounding expression.

sections.title: What it does not capture
sections.body: stderr is not captured unless you explicitly redirect it. A program that writes downloaded data only to a file gives you no response body through $(...).

sections.title: wget example
sections.body: wget normally downloads into a file. The argument -O - means 'write downloaded data to stdout'; it is the two-part form of -O-. The -q flag is optional and only controls progress and diagnostics.

sections.title: Memory and size
sections.body: Avoid storing very large downloaded files in a shell variable. A file is often a better choice, especially for binary data.

examples.description: Capture the HTTP response body rather than the wget progress messages.

practice: Use $(...) instead of legacy backticks for readability.
Quote the URL and the variable expansion.

topics.name: regex + * ?
topics.description: In Extended Regex, quantifiers act on the preceding character, class, or group. Their meaning is different from Bash arithmetic operators.

sections.title: Extended Regex quantifiers
sections.body: The operator affects the PRECEDING element:

items.definition: One or more a characters: a, aa, aaa, etc.
Zero or more a characters: empty text, a, aa, etc.
Zero or one a character.
Between two and four a characters.
One or more digits.
One or more occurrences of the group ab.

sections.title: Bash arithmetic is different
sections.body: Bash's + inside $((...)) means arithmetic addition. += can update a variable in an arithmetic context. This has nothing to do with regex repetition.

sections.title: Use the correct regex flavor
sections.body: Use grep -E for the ERE syntax shown here. Plain grep uses BRE, where + and ? are not special unless the implementation supports extensions or escaping.

examples.description: Match lines made of one or more a characters.
Arithmetic + adds numbers rather than matching text.

practice: Check the regex flavor before assuming a symbol has the same behavior.

topics.name: globs vs regex
topics.description: Bash glob patterns and regex both match text, but use different syntax and operate in different places.

sections.title: Bash globs
sections.body: Filename globs are expanded by Bash before running a command. The pattern *.txt matches filenames ending in .txt; the * stands for any sequence of characters.

sections.title: Regex
sections.body: In regex, * repeats the PRECEDING element. The regex .* means any number of arbitrary characters. Unlike a glob, a regex used by grep matches text inside files.

sections.title: Why quoting changes behavior
sections.body: Quoting '*.txt' prevents Bash from expanding the glob, which is correct when you want a program such as find -name to receive the pattern itself.

sections.title: An easy distinction
sections.body: ls *.txt lets Bash expand filenames first. find . -name '*.txt' lets find interpret its own filename pattern. grep -E '\.txt$' searches text for a .txt suffix.

examples.description: Pass a literal glob pattern to find.

practice: Do not interchange regex and glob syntax; they are different pattern languages.
